props.title: The House by the Cemetery

sections.content: **The House by the Cemetery** (1981) stands as one of Lucio Fulci's most atmospheric gothic horror films, blending his signature graphic violence with haunting supernatural elements. Following The Beyond (1981) and City of the Living Dead (1980), it completed Fulci's unofficial "Gates of Hell" trilogy. The film's unsettling atmosphere draws from classic gothic traditions established in **The Haunting** (1963) and **The Innocents** (1961), while its basement-dwelling monster Dr. Freudstein feels like a grotesque callback to **Frankenstein** (1931)'s medical horrors.

sections.content: The film's New England setting pays homage to H.P. Lovecraft's work, particularly evident in the decrepit mansion and its dark secrets. Fulci's direction creates a dreamlike quality through his trademark extreme close-ups of eyes and deliberately paced tracking shots. The violence, while shocking, serves the story's gothic foundations about family curses and undead scientists. This approach influenced later haunted house films like **The People Under the Stairs** (1991) and **Crimson Peak** (2015).

The dubbing and child performance issues that plague the film actually enhance its surreal, nightmarish quality. Like **Suspiria** (1977) and **Phenomena** (1985), the awkward English dialogue creates an otherworldly atmosphere that suits the supernatural story. The basement sequences, with their practical effects and claustrophobic tension, demonstrate Fulci's ability to craft genuine horror beyond his famous gore setpieces. sections.content: **The House by the Cemetery** belongs to a rich tradition of Italian gothic horror that includes **Black Sunday** (1960) and **Castle of Blood** (1964). Fulci's film modernized the gothic formula by incorporating extreme gore and psychological elements that would influence directors like **Hellraiser** (1987)'s Clive Barker and **In the Mouth of Madness** (1994)'s John Carpenter.
